content: The Global Action for Measurement of Adolescent Health (GAMA) Advisory Group has identified 47 priority indicators to focus on the most critical adolescent health issues. These indicators are designed to complement existing monitoring frameworks, such as those of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health. Countries are encouraged to collect and utilize data on these indicators to track progress in improving adolescent health. A new approach to measuring adolescent well-being is being developed. This framework will be applicable at both global and country levels, encompassing multiple domains beyond health to provide a comprehensive perspective on adolescent well-being. Adolescence is a period of rapid physical, emotional, and social changes, which presents unique challenges for health and well-being programs. To address these challenges, it is essential to disaggregate data by five-year age groups and sex. Programs must monitor a full range of indicators, from inputs and processes to outputs, outcomes, and impacts, as these serve different purposes and answer distinct questions. Periodic evaluations of adolescent health programs should build on routinely collected monitoring data. Over the past decade, the World Health Organization (WHO) has conducted priority-setting exercises in adolescent health. These exercises help researchers and funders identify and prioritize areas requiring focused attention. Monitoring, evaluation, and research efforts to improve adolescent health and well-being should incorporate adolescents' perspectives. Increasingly, participatory methods led by youth are being employed, including engaging adolescents as active evaluators and researchers. In 2015, all United Nations Member States adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which includes 17 goals and 169 targets tracked by 232 unique indicators. Adolescents are recognized as a critical group for achieving many of these goals. However, they are often underrepresented in global indicator frameworks due to a lack of ageand sex-disaggregated data for the 10–19 age group. The Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030) emphasizes the importance of placing children and adolescents at the center of the SDGs. It aligns with 34 SDG indicators and includes an additional 26 indicators from global initiatives on reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health. In total, 43 of the Global Strategy’s indicators pertain to adolescent health. The GAMA Advisory Group, established by WHO in collaboration with UN H6+ partner agencies, consists of 16 global adolescent health experts. Its objectives include providing technical guidance to define a core set of adolescent health indicators and promoting harmonized guidance for adolescent health measurement. This supports countries and technical organizations in collecting meaningful data to track progress in improving adolescent health. A consensus list of priority indicators with metadata has been developed through structured input from a wide range of stakeholders. These indicators build on existing initiatives, such as the SDGs and the Global Strategy, and ensure coverage of the most important health issues for adolescents. Some indicators were adapted to specify the 10–19 age range. The UN H6+ Technical Working Group on Adolescent Health and Well-Being has developed a definition and conceptual framework for adolescent well-being. The proposed definition, Adolescents thrive and are able to achieve their full potential, is supported by five domains: good health and optimal nutrition; connectedness, positive values, and societal contribution; safety and a supportive environment; learning, competence, education, skills, and employability; and agency and resilience. WHO, in collaboration with PMNCH and UN partners, is leading the development of a measurement approach for adolescent well-being, identifying priority indicators to support countries in gathering critical data. Many adolescent health-related indicators are derived from nationally representative household surveys, such as the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), or school-based health surveys like the Global School-Based Student Health Survey. Civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems are also important data sources, as they register births and deaths and provide vital statistics, including causes of death. National health information systems (NHIS) generate data to inform decision-making at all levels of the health system. Global adolescent health databases, such as WHO’s Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health and Ageing Data portal, UNICEF’s Adolescent Data Portal, and UNFPA’s Adolescent and Youth Dashboard, compile and display data on key indicators. These portals provide up-to-date global, regional, and country-level data, highlight data gaps, and allow for visualization and downloading of information. Monitoring equity and adolescents’ rights is critically important. Health determinants, risks, protective factors, and outcomes are rarely distributed equally across populations, and health programs reach subpopulations to varying degrees. For example, insufficient physical activity among adolescents varies significantly by age, sex, rural or urban residence, and school attendance. Ignoring these differences risks leaving the needs of specific subpopulations unaddressed. Surveys often exclude out-of-school adolescents, who may be at the greatest risk in terms of health behaviors and outcomes. Monitoring inequality and disaggregating data by age, sex, disability, socioeconomic status, and other dimensions is essential to address these disparities effectively.
